content: The provided text is a detailed list of treatment regimens for various infections and conditions, formatted in a fragmented and encoded manner. 1. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Retinitis in HIV-Infected Adults Treatment options include intravenous ganciclovir, oral valganciclovir, intravenous foscarnet, intravenous cidofovir, or a combination of a ganciclovir intraocular implant with oral valganciclovir. 2. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Retinitis in HIV-Infected Infants and Children Initial treatment (induction therapy) involves intravenous ganciclovir for acquired CMV disease, including CMV retinitis and other end-organ disseminated CMV diseases such as colitis, esophagitis, and central nervous system (CNS) disease. For ganciclovir-resistant CMV infections, intravenous foscarnet is an alternative. 3. CMV in Transplant Patients The preferred regimen for CMV prophylaxis or treatment in transplant patients is oral valganciclovir. 4. CMV Colitis and Esophagitis Preferred regimen: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily for 14–21 days, followed by 900 mg once daily for maintenance therapy. Alternative regimen: Intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 14–21 days, with an extended induction period of 3–6 weeks in some cases. Maintenance therapy may not be necessary except after relapse. Responses to treatment are less predictable compared to CMV retinitis. 5. CMV Pneumonia Preferred regimen: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 900 mg once daily for maintenance therapy. Alternative regimens include intravenous ganciclovir, intravenous foscarnet, or intravenous cidofovir, with appropriate hydration and adjunctive medications such as oral probenecid. 6. CMV Encephalitis and Ventriculitis Treatment regimens are similar to those for CMV retinitis, with intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet as primary options. 7. Lumbosacral Polyradiculopathy The preferred treatment is intravenous ganciclovir, as used for CMV retinitis. Foscarnet is another option, and switching to oral valganciclovir is recommended when feasible. 8. Prevention of Opportunistic Infections in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) Preemptive therapy involves weekly monitoring of CMV viremia using PCR or antigenemia assays from days 10 to 100 post-transplant. Treatment is initiated if CMV is detected. Traditional prophylaxis includes intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 7–14 days, followed by 5 mg/kg once daily for 5 days per week until day 100 or for at least 3 weeks. Alternatively, prophylaxis can be administered from engraftment to day 100 using intravenous ganciclovir. 9. Prevention of Opportunistic Infections in Solid Organ Transplantation (SOT) For kidney, kidney/pancreas, and heart transplant recipients, oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily is recommended, starting by day 10 and continuing until at least day 100. For liver transplant recipients, intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir is used with caution. For lung transplant recipients, intravenous ganciclovir is administered for 5–7 days, followed by oral valganciclovir for 3–6 months. 10. Post-Treatment Suppression for CMV Retinitis For patients with a CD4 count <100/mm³, oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily is the preferred maintenance therapy. 11. Supportive Therapy for Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) Due to Coronavirus Careful fluid management is essential to avoid capillary leakage. Supplemental oxygen should be provided for hypoxic patients. Intubation and mechanical ventilation equipment should be readily available due to the potential for rapid respiratory failure. There is no specific antiviral treatment for hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS); management remains supportive. 12. Hepatitis E Virus Hepatitis E is usually self-limiting, and hospitalization is generally not required. Hospitalization is necessary for fulminant hepatitis or symptomatic pregnant women. 13. Rotavirus-Induced Diarrhea Zinc supplementation reduces the duration of diarrhea by 25% and stool volume by 30%. Severe dehydration or shock requires intravenous rehydration. Nutrient-rich foods, including breast milk, should be continued during episodes to break the cycle of malnutrition and diarrhea. Prevention includes access to safe drinking water, improved sanitation, handwashing, and rotavirus vaccination. 14. Rhinovirus Treatment Symptomatic relief can be achieved with intranasal ipratropium bromide and oral clemastine. Oral pleconaril, if administered within 24 hours of symptom onset, reduces the duration and severity of cold symptoms. 15. Bacterial Meningitis For methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), intravenous nafcillin or oxacillin is preferred. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), intravenous vancomycin is the treatment of choice, with alternatives including linezolid or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. 16. Septic Thrombosis of Cavernous or Dural Venous Sinus For MRSA, intravenous vancomycin is the preferred treatment, with alternatives such as linezolid or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Surgical evaluation for drainage of contiguous infection sites is recommended. 17. Acute Conjunctivitis Due to MRSA Topical vancomycin ointment (1%) applied four times daily is the preferred treatment. 18. Appendicitis and Diverticulitis with Complicated Intra-Abdominal Infections For MRSA, intravenous vancomycin is the preferred treatment. 19. Cystic Fibrosis with Staphylococcus aureus Infection For MSSA, intravenous nafcillin or oxacillin is recommended. For MRSA, intravenous vancomycin or linezolid is preferred. 20. Bronchiectasis with Staphylococcus aureus Infection For MSSA, oral flucloxacillin is the first-line treatment. For MRSA, rifampicin combined with trimethoprim or doxycycline is recommended.
